newsitem.title: PERU: FEATURE-Latin America's youngest first lady a star in Peru.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Latin America's youngest first lady a star in Peru.

text.p: Seated in front of a huge, pink plastic phallus at a health fair, Keiko Fujimori had her composure tested as she resisted giggling in front of cameramen eager to snap an undignified photograph of Latin America's youngest first lady.

Only 21 but with two years experience already as Peru's leading woman, she dutifully received personal instruction on how to wear a condom correctly in the pitch for birth control and managed to steal the paparazzi's fire. "Take this. You might learn something," she said, handing sex education pamphlets to the cameramen who pursued her as she visited a health fair in one of Lima's sprawling shantytowns.

Her ordeal over, the first lady ran to the familiar solace of Wendy, one of the friends who provide constant reassurance as she carries out state duties normally reserved for women more than twice her age. "Did you see what they did to me?" she screamed as she burst out laughing.

Unlike her publicity-seeking father President Alberto Fujimori, Keiko Fujimori, who was thrust into the role of first lady following her parents' turbulent and public divorce, is not a natural in the limelight. "At times I'm in the middle of a speech, I look up and see all the people in front of me and think, 'Oh no. I can't go on,'" she said back in her office at Government Palace.

Her parents' separation and eventual divorce last year captivated Peru like a soap opera as Fujimori locked his wife, Susana Higuchi, out of the palace and she launched her own opposition party accusing her husband of corruption.

Keiko Fujimori, rising "from the ashes of a lost love," as Higuchi said, was also burned by the traumatic divorce. Wary of the country's appetite for scandal, she is more reserved in public life. "I have learned to be more cautious. I used to be open with everybody but now I am cautious," she said.

Most of the year she studies business administration at Boston University, and back home she avoids the histrionics of her parents, trying to keep a low profile. As one of the world's youngest first ladies, she strives to keep attention on the social programmes she supervises in a country where half of the 24 million inhabitants live in poverty and most of the workforce is without a proper job.
"We are in Peru and Peru needs a lot of help," she said. "I see a lot of children smiling, but not all of them. I'd like to see them all happy."

An unpretentious and hard-working young woman, she still cut a pop-star figure in her black, flowing suit, flanked throughout the shantytown visit by impish children clamouring for an autograph. "She's beautiful," said 12-year-old Jhonny Cerquin. "A bit fat, but beautiful."

While her father blazes his publicity trail through Peru's peasant regions, forcing photo opportunities wherever he can, Keiko Fujimori is more modest. If he directs the show, she is carried along by it. She strides through the dusty town of 20,000 amid chants of "Keiko, Keiko" with a curious look in her eyes that shows she does not quite believe the adulation.

But the eldest of President Fujimori's four children also leaves the clear impression she has her feet on the ground. When she needs a drink to cool off, nurses scurry off in search of a glass, only to find the first lady is happy enough to swig from the bottle like everybody else.

"She's got an ability to get on with people. She puts them at their ease," said Carmen Maldonado, vice president of the Childrens' Foundation, which, with the first lady's patronage, provides orphanages for around 2,400 abandoned children.

Nor has being in the public eye made her vain. She responds with disarming calm to unkind television satire that constantly makes jibes about her weight. "It doesn't bother me. I am chubby," she said.

In Boston, fellow students do not know that once she leaves for summer break she is normally rushing from one Andean village to another, inspecting the charities she sponsors or attending official ceremonies with world dignitaries. And back in Lima, despite the permanent presence of her nine bodyguards, she tries to keep her life normal, going to the movies, soccer matches and discos with the friends she has kept since high school.

Public life may mean she sacrifices her privacy but it is the Machiavellian nature of politics she most dislikes about her work. Straitjacketed by the need to maintain her father's well-managed image, the normally comfortable Keiko Fujimori is awkwardly terse fielding questions about her father's six-year administration.

And she is adamant that she will leave politics once her father gives up the presidency. Her aversion stems from a conviction that it was self-interested politicians who provoked her parents' split-up.
"People around them, really awful people, had a big influence, advising them badly. That is what ruined the marriage. That's why I don't like politics," she said.
